entry.englishMeaning: to an important or noticeable degree
entry.coreIdea: Enough to make a noticeable or important difference.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Degree adverb meaning by an important or noticeable amount; here, a meaningful change in input data.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Neutral: the change could be helpful or harmful depending on what changed.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Investigative here: the question asks whether the amount of change matters.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Neutral to formal, common in reports and technical discussion. The sentence does not establish a formal statistical-significance test.

when_to_use: Describe a change or difference that is important or clearly noticeable.
Compare amounts using significantly higher, lower, larger or smaller when the difference deserves attention.
when_not_to_use: For a tiny change that does not matter in context, slightly may be more accurate.
Do not treat the word alone as proof that a formal statistical test was performed.

advanced_nuance: What counts as an important difference depends on the situation; significantly gives no fixed percentage. Add figures when precision matters.

In a statistical discussion, significantly may refer to a test result. The saved question alone does not establish that technical use; this lesson follows the stored meaning of an important or noticeable degree.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: A change big enough to notice or take into account.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: The revised estimate is significantly higher than the original.
memory_practice.recall_question: What is the difference in grammar between a significant change and changed significantly?
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which sentence correctly describes degree: The cost increased significantly, or The cost increased significant? Explain the word form.
memory_practice.production_task: Write a sentence comparing two waiting times or costs using significantly. Add enough context to show why the difference matters.

examples.example_1: The waiting time fell significantly after the team added another service desk.
examples.example_2: The revised estimate is significantly higher than the amount we first planned to spend.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Has the input data changed significantly?
B: Yes. Many more records now come from new customers.
A: Then we should examine how that affects our results.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: Has the input data changed significantly?
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to an important or noticeable degree
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The speaker asks whether the input data has changed enough to matter. The sentence does not state a numerical threshold or report a statistical test.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: The waiting time changed significant.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say The waiting time changed significantly. Use the adverb to describe the degree of change.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Significant is an adjective: a significant change. Significantly is an adverb: changed significantly or significantly different.

semanticReview.finding: Ordinary degree meaning retained; adverb grammar repaired and unsupported statistical-test inference avoided.

entry.pronunciation: Approximate pronunciation: un-der-per-FORM. Capitals show stress; this is text guidance, not audio.
entry.englishMeaning: to perform less well than expected or required
entry.coreIdea: Achieve less than the expected standard.

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Abstract verb for achieving less than an expected standard.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Negative evaluation of performance, without necessarily judging someone's character or effort.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Direct and problem-focused here: underperformance is listed among situations to address promptly.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common workplace and performance-review wording. State the expected standard and evidence to avoid a vague personal judgement.

when_to_use: Describe work or results that fall below a stated expectation or requirement.
Discuss a team, employee or project in relation to an agreed standard.
when_not_to_use: Do not use underperform to mean someone refuses to work; poor results do not by themselves show unwillingness.
Avoid using it as a label for a person’s overall worth. Identify the work and standard being discussed.

advanced_nuance: Underperform is a relative judgement: the same result may exceed one target and fall below another. Make the comparison clear.
When discussing people, the word can sound critical. Specific evidence and attention to resources make the feedback more useful than a general personal label.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: Results below the line marking the expected standard.
memory_practice.memory_sentence: A team may underperform when it lacks the tools it needs.
memory_practice.recall_question: Why should you name the expected standard when saying that a team underperforms?
memory_practice.recognition_task: A team produces useful work but falls short of its agreed target. Can it underperform even though it completes some work? Explain.
memory_practice.production_task: Write two respectful sentences about a fictional team that may underperform. State the expectation and one possible reason without assuming laziness.

examples.example_1: A team may underperform when its targets are unclear or it lacks the tools it needs.
examples.example_2: If I underperform in this role, I want specific feedback about what needs to improve.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: Why does the team underperform against its delivery targets?
B: We need to check whether the deadlines and staffing are realistic.
A: Let us compare the actual results with the agreed targets.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: If  an  employee  underperform s,  fa ils  to  live  up  to  a  promi se,  doesn't  carry  his  or  her  fair  share,  or  simply isn't  productive  enough,  the  affe cted  parties  address  the  problem  immediat ely.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to perform less well than expected or required
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: The writer discusses an employee whose work falls below expectations and says the affected people address the problem promptly. The extracted text has spacing errors, including underperform s; these are not standard spelling.

mistakes_differences.common_mistake: Incorrect: The team is underperform this month.
mistakes_differences.correction: Say The team is underperforming this month for an ongoing situation, or The team underperforms for a general pattern.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Underperform means fall below an expectation. Fail can mean not achieve a particular goal at all; underperforming does not necessarily mean producing no useful results.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: person/team/project + underperform(s); underperform + in + area; underperform + against + target

semanticReview.finding: Performance judged against an explicit standard, without implying laziness or total failure; source OCR spacing disclosed.

entry.englishMeaning: to make contact to see how someone is doing
entry.coreIdea: A small contact signal saying how are things?

meaning_usage_profile.meaning_type: Conversational phrasal verb for making contact to ask how someone is doing; here, follow up after a first day.
meaning_usage_profile.connotation: Supportive here: the contact is presented as interest in the person's experience.
meaning_usage_profile.tone: Friendly and reassuring: the speaker commits to checking how the first day went.
meaning_usage_profile.register: Common in everyday and workplace conversation. This entry does not teach hotel registration or airport check-in.

when_to_use: Make brief contact to ask how someone is doing, especially after a new experience or a difficult day.
when_not_to_use: Check in with someone makes contact; check someone in registers their arrival.
A friendly check-in should give room for an honest answer rather than demand a positive report.

advanced_nuance: A friendly check-in should give room for an honest answer rather than demand a positive report.
Check in with someone does not specify whether you call, send a message or speak in person; the situation determines the method.

memory_practice.memory_trigger: A small contact signal saying how are things?
memory_practice.memory_sentence: I will check in with my cousin after her first day at college.
memory_practice.production_task: Arrange a supportive follow-up with a new colleague. Respond in one or two natural sentences using the expression, then compare with the pattern after answering.
memory_practice.recall_question: Recall the expression for this meaning without looking: to make contact to see how someone is doing. Explain its function in one sentence.
memory_practice.recognition_task: Which option fits the taught meaning and standard construction? A: I will check in with you tomorrow. B: I will check you in tomorrow, meaning contact you. Explain your choice, then check the correction and distinction.

examples.scenario: I will check in with you tomorrow to see how the first day went.
examples.another_setting: I will check in with my cousin after her first day at college.

natural_examples.mini_conversation:
A: I will check in with my cousin after her first day at college.
B: Ask whether she found the right classroom.

meaning_in_context.source_sentence: I will check in with you tomorrow to see how the first day went.
meaning_in_context.contextual_meaning: to make contact to see how someone is doing
meaning_in_context.simple_explanation: A small contact signal saying how are things? Check in with someone makes contact; check someone in registers their arrival.

mistakes_differences.correction: I will check in with you tomorrow.
mistakes_differences.common_mistake: I will check you in tomorrow, meaning contact you.
mistakes_differences.important_difference: Check in with someone makes contact; check someone in registers their arrival.

patterns_collocations.main_pattern: check in: check in with + person
